About Cosmic Scale

An interactive tour of size: from planets and moons, through the stars and nebulae of the Milky Way, out to the cosmic web and the edge of the observable universe.
Created by Allen Vincent · allenvincent808.github.io

Acknowledgments

This project was built in collaboration with Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic. Allen came up with the concept, set the direction and features, and reviewed each version. Claude wrote the code, a custom WebGL renderer with no external libraries, and helped research and cross-check the scientific data against the sources below. Any remaining errors are ours, and corrections are welcome.
Thanks also to the scientists and institutions who make their data freely available: NASA, JPL, ESA, the International Astronomical Union, and the many astronomers whose catalogues and papers are listed here. The approach is inspired by Charles and Ray Eames's film Powers of Ten (1977).

How accurate is it?

From real catalogues and measurements (almost everything): planet, moon and spacecraft positions; 510 asteroids, comets and dwarf planets on their real orbits for any date; 109,400 stars with measured distances and the real naked-eye night sky; 6,476 open clusters, 196 globular clusters and 4,253 pulsars; dozens of named stars and nebulae; 10,936 galaxies with measured distances plus ~200 described galaxies; and the true sizes and distances in the Everyday-scale panel.
Illustrative (each can be switched off): the Oort cloud, which has never been observed directly; the spiral-arm model of the whole Milky Way, because no survey has mapped the far side of our galaxy (Gaia has measured about 2 billion of its 100–400 billion stars, mostly near us); and the distant cosmic web beyond about 1.5 billion light-years, where no complete 3D catalogue exists. A few remaining features (the CMB pattern, the galaxy textures of the planets) are artistic.
Known limits: galaxy distances in the big catalogue come mostly from redshifts, which stretch clusters along our line of sight (the "fingers of God") and carry 5–20% uncertainty; the strip with no galaxies is the "zone of avoidance" hidden behind the Milky Way's dust; only the brightest 510 of the ~1.4 million known asteroids are shown.

References

Solar System

  1. Williams, D. R. Planetary Fact Sheet. NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA), Goddard Space Flight Center. Diameters, rotation periods, axial tilts.
  2. Seidelmann, P. K. (ed.) (1992). Explanatory Supplement to the Astronomical Almanac, Table 5.8.1. University Science Books. J2000 mean orbital elements of the planets.
  3. Jacobson, R. A. et al. Planetary Satellite Mean Elements. JPL Solar System Dynamics, NASA. Moon orbits.
  4. Laskar, J. & Jacobson, R. A. (1987). GUST86: an analytical ephemeris of the Uranian satellites. Astronomy & Astrophysics, 188, 212–224.
  5. Minor Planet Center (IAU) and NASA Solar System Exploration: moon counts (as of mid-2026).
  6. NASA/JPL Voyager mission status (distances of Voyager 1 and 2).
  7. NASA Science, Solar System Exploration: Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud overviews (Oort cloud ≈ 2,000–100,000 AU).

Stars, nebulae and the Milky Way

  1. IAU Working Group on Star Names (WGSN). IAU Catalog of Star Names, including Rigil Kentaurus, Toliman and Proxima Centauri.
  2. European Space Agency. The Hipparcos and Tycho Catalogues (1997) and Gaia Collaboration data releases: stellar distances and the J2000 galactic-coordinate transformation.
  3. Basant, R. et al. (2025). Four sub-Earth planets orbiting Barnard's Star from MAROON-X and ESPRESSO. Astrophysical Journal Letters, 982, L1.
  4. NASA / ESA Hubble Space Telescope: Hubble's Messier Catalog (nebula and galaxy distances).
  5. Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration (2022). First Sagittarius A* results. Astrophysical Journal Letters, 930, L12.

Galaxies and large-scale structure

  1. McConnachie, A. W. (2012). The observed properties of dwarf galaxies in and around the Local Group. Astronomical Journal, 144, 4, and the updated online Nearby Dwarf Galaxy Database. Local Group positions.
  2. Compiled distances: "List of nearest galaxies", Wikipedia (citing primary literature), checked against NASA values where available.
  3. Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration (2019). First M87 Event Horizon Telescope results. Astrophysical Journal Letters, 875, L1.
  4. Tully, R. B., Courtois, H., Hoffman, Y. & Pomarède, D. (2014). The Laniakea supercluster of galaxies. Nature, 513, 71–73.
  5. Gott, J. R. et al. (2005). A map of the universe. Astrophysical Journal, 624, 463 (Sloan Great Wall).
  6. Planck Collaboration (2020). Planck 2018 results VI: cosmological parameters. Astronomy & Astrophysics, 641, A6. Age of the universe and the observable-universe radius.
  7. Zwicky, F. (1933). Die Rotverschiebung von extragalaktischen Nebeln. Helvetica Physica Acta, 6, 110–127 (Coma Cluster and dark matter).

Catalogues used for the data points

  1. Nash, D. (Astronexus). HYG Database, v4.1 — Hipparcos, Yale Bright Star and Gliese catalogues combined. CC BY-SA 4.0.
  2. Steinicke, W. (2006). Revised NGC and IC Catalog; and Karachentsev, I. D. et al. (2004). A catalog of neighboring galaxies. Astronomical Journal, 127, 2031 — as compiled in the Celestia project's galaxy catalogue (GPL-2.0-or-later).
  3. Perren, G. I., Pera, M. S., Navone, H. D. & Vázquez, R. A. (2023). The Unified Cluster Catalogue. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 526, 4107 (open clusters; via Celestia, CC BY 4.0).
  4. Baumgardt, H. et al. (2023). Fundamental parameters of Galactic globular clusters database (via Celestia, GPL-2.0-or-later).
  5. Manchester, R. N., Hobbs, G. B., Teoh, A. & Hobbs, M. (2005). The ATNF Pulsar Catalogue. Astronomical Journal, 129, 1993 (v2.6.3; via Celestia, CC BY 4.0).
  6. Minor-body orbital elements from the IAU Minor Planet Center and JPL Small-Body Database, as packaged by the Stellarium (ssystem_minor.ini) and Celestia projects (GPL-2.0-or-later).

Software and design

  1. WebGL 2 (Khronos Group): all graphics are rendered with a custom engine and no third-party libraries.
  2. Thanks to the open-source Celestia and Stellarium communities, whose curated catalogues made this possible.
  3. Typefaces: Space Grotesk and JetBrains Mono, via Google Fonts (SIL Open Font License).
Version 4 · November 2026. Because some catalogue data is GPL-licensed and HYG is CC BY-SA, this page is shared under GPL-3.0. For educational use. Built with Claude by Anthropic.
